data.title: Income Investing: 6 Safe Dividend Stocks For Volatile Times — Barron's
How the Midterms Give the Fed More Room to Maneuver — Barron's
Funds: This ETF Makes It Easy to Invest In Hard Assets — Barron's
data.description:
By Lewis Braham

Hard assets like commodities are known to be a good hedge against inflation, but how do you decide how much to be in gold, oil, or real estate? In today's volatile macroeconomic environment, it's an important but difficult question.

The VanEck Real Assets exchange-traded fund does the allocating to hard assets for you. The $1.4 billion ETF has delivered a stellar 11.5% five-year annualized return, versus the 7.5% average of its peers in Morningstar's moderately aggressive allocation fund category. It has performed well during inflationary panics, rising 1.8% in 2022 when the S&P 500 fell 18.1%, and it fell significantly less during the tariff panic in 2025. It has a 0.55% expense ratio — reasonable for an actively managed fund.

"Our objective with this strategy is to deliver the most complete real-asset solution possible in a balanced and risk-managed way," lead manager David Schassler says. To do that, Schassler and co-manager John Lau employ quantitative indicators that track the price trends of commodities and other real assets, macroeconomic data, and underlying investor sentiment to determine their asset targets.

Rather than relying on static long-term allocations, Schassler invests in three main asset buckets, with flexible exposure ranges depending on the market and economic environment. The "growth assets" bucket, which includes commodity futures and natural-resource equities, does well when economies are growing and products like oil and industrial metals are needed to build and operate factories and equipment. This can range from 30% to 60% of the ETF's portfolio, and is currently 40%.

Such natural resources, Schassler argues, are necessary for the massive artificial-intelligence buildout that is driving global growth. In addition to holding energy equity stakes in oil refiners like Marathon Petroleum and Valero Energy, the fund gains direct commodity exposure via futures contracts. It currently has a 26% weighting in VanEck Commodity Strategy, a futures-driven ETF that Schassler also manages successfully, having beaten 99% of his peers in Morningstar's commodities broad basket category in the past five years.

Futures can provide returns not just via commodity exposure but also through astute positioning on their expiration-date curves, which resemble bond yield curves. Schassler often sells an expiring near-term futures contract at a high price and uses the proceeds to buy a cheaper, longer-dated futures contract. The spread between the two prices is called a "roll yield." This adds to the fund's return and helps to avoid short-term commodity price disruptions, as the shortest-dated front-month futures are the most sensitive to a commodity's current spot price. Schassler will also adjust the expiration date exposure of contracts depending on his bullishness or defensiveness on particular commodities.

Thus, though the underlying commodity ETF is currently 55% in energy futures, lately Schassler has been buying back-month contracts, which are less sensitive to oil prices, in anticipation of the Iran war ending and oil prices finally coming down. He has also diversified the fund's energy futures beyond crude into refined oil, natural gas, diesel, and heating fuel, each of which has different sensitivities to the macroeconomic backdrop.

The "income-producing assets" bucket, currently 36% of the Real Asset ETF's portfolio, can range from 15% to 50% and includes master limited partnerships, infrastructure stocks, utilities, and real estate investment trusts. Schassler is less interested in individual stocks within these industries than in owning baskets of stocks of the largest, most reputable companies in them, and adjusting his overall weightings to these baskets based on market conditions. His largest income industry weighting recently was 8.2% in energy pipeline MLPs like Enterprise Products Partners, while REITs like Welltower were the smallest at only 2.8%.

"If we went to a different, more bearish regime, you would expect us to naturally pivot toward REITs, potentially utilities, and infrastructure," Schassler notes. Conversely, in an inflationary environment driven by supply shocks, the playbook shifts. Rising inflation devalues fixed income and compresses equity multiples across traditionally defensive segments like REITs, while MLP oil and natural-gas pipelines see surging revenue.

Although the ETF will probably take some short-term lumps if the war in Iran ends and oil falls, Schassler actually thinks it would be good for his long-term AI-driven growth narrative. If oil is priced too high, it will stymie that growth. A decline in inflation and interest rates will also benefit the income-oriented portion of the fund, as these assets are competing with bonds that offer elevated interest rates because of the war.

"Higher energy prices at the levels that we're talking about create demand destruction," Schassler says. "In addition, upward pressure on inflation puts upward pressure on interest rates. The expectation [if oil prices fall] would be that we would lose money on the commodities, and we'd make money in a lot of other places. "

One area that would benefit from falling oil and interest rates is gold. The precious metal pays no income, so investors will often opt for bonds instead of gold when real inflation-adjusted rates are high on bonds, like today. Gold and cash fall into the ETF's "capital preservation" bucket, which can range from 15% to 30% of the portfolio and is currently 23%. Bullion itself, which the ETF owns via its position in the VanEck Merk Gold ETF, is 18%.

"Gold is the original store-of-value asset," Schassler says. "During periods of financial excess, during periods of [currency] debasement, during periods of persistent and elevated inflation like what we've been experiencing now for the past five years, that embedded scarcity really comes to life."

Yet like everything else, Schassler will adjust his gold position based on market conditions. Bullion got as high as 24% of the ETF by the end of 2025, but Schassler cut it back to add to oil and other commodities before the Iran war started this year. "Gold was structurally overbought," he says. "It was performing exceptionally well, and was encompassing more and more of our total risk budget. So, we reallocated from gold to energy, which we were structurally underweight."

Having that nuanced and balanced approach toward real assets is what makes this ETF so useful as a diversification tool.

data.title: Energy Drinks Are Exploding. Why Is Celsius Stock Fizzling? — Barron's
data.description:
By Jack Hough

Alani Nu just passed Celsius. Those are energy drinks, not trending baby names, at least as far as I know. By "energy drinks," I mean the endless rows of caffeinated cans that have taken over America's convenience store coolers with a subtle zombie-Teletubby-yoga-firefight aesthetic.

These two brands are owned by the same company, Celsius Holdings, which returned 28,000% from its 2015 turnaround to its 2024 peak. Since then, shares have fallen by two-thirds. Investment bank Stephens cut its price target on the stock in late October, but still rates it at Overweight and Volatile, which I identify with. Deutsche Bank cut it to Hold in August, citing competitive crowding.

In the U.S. alone, energy drinks are a $25 billion industry, putting them between soda and bottled water, and way ahead of sports drinks like Gatorade. They've moved beyond their traditional core of college students, gamers, and long-haul truckers, to wellness-minded moms and TikTok-influenced teens, among others. If you aren't familiar with the major players, here's a briefing:

Red Bull (launched 1987; 80 milligrams of caffeine per standard can, like a cup of coffee): Industry pioneer, privately held in Austria. Makes roughly as much money as Chipotle Mexican Grill. Preferred by first-year investment bankers, the skydiving-curious, vodka-mixing clubbers.

Monster (2002; 160mg, or 300mg for Reign version): Tallboy cans with neon green claw marks favored by nightshift workers, elite Call of Duty forces, actual military, and Planet Fitness grunters. Owned by Monster Beverage, once a tiny natural-soda company, now one of history's best-performing stocks, up 100,000%. Really.

Celsius (2004, relaunched 2015; 200mg): Sterile, white, slim cans with fruit illustrations and references to ginger-root-this and thermogenic-that, favored by Peloton owners and pilates instructors who'd like to make clear that they would never, ever, try Monster. Saved by billionaire "vitamin king" Carl DeSantis, who transformed the brand from a diet aid to a fitness beverage. Distributed by PepsiCo, which owns a stake.

C4 Energy (2011 in powder tubs, 2018 as canned drinks; 200mg standard, 300mg Ultimate): Hazard-yellow cans with bomb graphics sold in gym coolers to men who can bench their bodyweight, plus yours. Contains beta-alanine, which binds to something and does muscly stuff, but is better known for its side effect, tingling of the skin. Distributed by Keurig Dr Pepper, which owns a stake.

Alani Nu (2018; 200mg): Whimsical pastel cans with candy themes and flavors. Favored by Gen Z women and overwhelmed parents who just can't do another argument with their teen today about energy drinks, so for now they'll just grab a coupon-discounted case at BJ's Wholesale rather than paying $4 a pop at the Mobil Mart. Bought by Celsius last year for $1.8 billion.

Ghost Energy (2020; 200mg): Cartoony cans with flavor tie-ins like Sour Patch and Bubblicious, favored by extreme sneakerheads and the PlayStation warrior who just took out that Monster drinker who had no business trying Fortnight. Go back to Call of Duty, boomer.

There are many more insurgent brands with elaborate niche positioning, like Gorilla Mind, from a YouTube biohacker, with nootropics, which are said to increase cerebral blah-blah and modulate neuro hidey-ho. There are celebrity drinks, like ZOA Energy from Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson. Some have aggressive names, like Full Throttle and Venom. I don't know much about Bawls Guarana, but I've confirmed that it's a beverage, not a topical treatment. There's Cocaine Energy, Pimp Juice, Whoop Ass, and others we probably shouldn't print here.

If you want my top recommendation, make coffee at home and breathe dragon breath on your loved ones until you brush your teeth in the morning, the way God intended. Also, a note for Gen Z: I support everything you're saying about how the cost of living has gotten out of control, and young people can barely afford cars, to say nothing of houses. But it distracts from the argument if you're double-fisting cans of Spike Shooter. A two-drink-a-day habit at $3.50 each comes out to more than $12,000 over five years, or perhaps $15,000 invested in stocks.

I'm no biohacker, but some of these things look thermonuclear. That brand I just mentioned packs 350mg of caffeine into an 8.4 ounce can. Regulatory guidance varies by country, but 400mg is a commonly cited ceiling for adults; 100mg for adolescents; and zero for kids under 12. Too much caffeine can cause arrhythmia and tachycardia, which are well-known sea monsters from Homer's Odyssey.

What keeps energy drinks from falling into a price war for now is that most of the revenue comes from impulse decisions at convenience stores. At warehouse clubs, discounting is rife. When Stephens analyst Jim Salera cut his price target on Celsius last month from $50 to $46, he cited the rising cost of aluminum and fuel, and softness in the core brand. But his new target still works out to more than 50% upside from recent levels.

Salera finds several things to like. First, valuation. Celsius stock recently traded at 18 times forward earnings projections, versus a jittery 37 times, on average, over the past three years. Second, guzzle velocity. The energy-drink industry is growing sales at 15% a year, the fastest in the beverage aisle. Third, warehouse heft. Red Bull and Celsius are bullying smaller brands at Costco Wholesale. Fourth, young ladies. Alani Nu is bringing them in.

Buying the shares here could qualify as what Wall Street calls catching a falling knife, which is only slightly riskier than it sounds. I don't have a guess either way on the stock. Maybe I'll chug some nootropics until I feel more conviction. Better yet, meet me at Planet Fitness and let's discuss it over C4s until our faces tingle. I'm lucky if I can bench three digits these days, but I can still grunt with the best of them.

Write to Jack Hough at jack.hough@barrons.com and subscribe to his Barron's Streetwise podcast.

data.title: Don't Lose Sleep Over GLP-1s. This Stock Is Still a Bargain. — Barron's
data.description:
ResMed, the San Diego-based medical device maker, has proven its worth with sleep apnea patients. The stock is cheap, mainly over concerns that GLP-1 weight loss drugs will make ResMed's products less necessary. That means investors can buy into a growing market opportunity.

By Jacob Sonenshine

Behind the opportunity is continued adoption of continuous positive airway pressure, or CPAP, products. These masks and other devices are critical for sleep apnea patients. Almost one billion people worldwide suffer from the condition, according to the National Library of Medicine. Tens of millions of them rely on ResMed's products.

Tens of millions of people are also on GLP-1s throughout the world. As they lose weight, their need for certain medical procedures and treatments declines. But the link to sleep apnea is still elusive.

GLP-1s don't seem "to reduce the number of people who we are seeing have an interest in CPAP," says Anita Shelgikar, a sleep medicine specialist affiliated with the University of Michigan. Patients can lose weight and still need CPAP.

Nor is obesity the only cause of sleep apnea. Some medicines such as sedatives, and even alcohol intake, can cause respiratory depression, supporting CPAP demand. And fluid can shift into a patient's neck at night and disrupt the airway when they lie down.

In fact, GLP-1s can even prove a tailwind to CPAP demand. "One thing these GLP medications have increased is the awareness of sleep apnea," says Shelgikar. "It has motivated people to pursue a sleep evaluation when otherwise they would not have."

Supporting that, ResMed CEO Mick Farrell said on the October earnings call that "we are still seeing that patients who have scripts for both CPAP and GLP-1s are more than 11% more likely to start on CPAP therapy than patients who have a script for CPAP alone."

Relatedly, the Democrats' sweep in midterm U.S. elections brings about a greater probability of tax incentives for Affordable Care Act access, which would boost demand for all sorts of goods — including GLP-1s, adding more fuel for the weight-loss growth story.

ResMed has beaten sales estimates in each of the past 12 quarters and has never reduced long-term growth guidance. Its fiscal year first quarter, reported in late October, showed 8.4% year-over-year sales growth to $1.45 billion when excluding currency fluctuations and the negative, one-time impact of lost revenue from the divestiture of MatrixCare, a software company focused on senior care facilities. That's in line with the high-single-digit growth it has seen in the past few years and the high-single-digit annual growth management said to expect over the coming five years, when it presented quarterly results in January.

The resulting sales growth can spur even more earnings growth because the operating margin can rise. ResMed hasn't changed its longstanding commitment to keep research and development at roughly 6.5% of revenue. It should rise as a percentage of revenue this year, with Chief Financial Officer Aaron Bloomer noting on the call that the company has prioritized investments in creating new, cutting-edge products.

That's why analysts forecast a 37% operating margin by 2030, up from 36% in fiscal 2027, according to FactSet.

Combine that with continued stock buybacks, and earnings per share can grow in the double-digit percentages. ResMed has a record of executing profitable growth, with enough cash left for repurchases. Earnings per share grew 17% in fiscal 2026, with margins rising a touch.

That's the type of profit growth the market should appreciate soon, as the company continues to execute. It often provides fairly low guidance, thereby setting its own bar low — and then beats Wall Street estimates. That, combined with no real evidence of demand destruction from GLP-1s, can catalyze stock gains.

"We think management is also baking in some conservatism," writes William Blair analyst Brandon Vazquez, who expects margin expansion and over 12% EPS growth in fiscal 2027.

Stable growth from the company's residential-care software business could aid the market's confidence in long-term growth. This business provides software applications that help nursing and care providers track patients' data, and helps ResMed maintain the competitiveness of its overall product offerings. Totaling $155 million, it grew 8% in the most recent quarter in constant currency, excluding the MatrixCare divestiture. Farrell said on the call to expect high-single-digit revenue growth and expanding margins in that segment.

The picture of strong earnings growth can lift the company's valuation. The stock trades at about 19 times next the next 12 months' earnings, only a point above the S&P 500's valuation. But with its durable EPS growth — higher than what investors expect from the index in the long term — it can trade more richly. It touched 26 times as recently as 2024.

Given the valuation, "risk/reward is favorable for a double-digit EPS grower," Vazquez writes.

Buying this name can help an investor sleep at night.

data.title: China Cranks Out New Drugs. How to Play It. — Barron's
data.description:
Many of the new drug treatments that created waves at a major cancer medicine conference last month were invented in China.

By Bill Alpert

Merck won plaudits at the European Society for Medical Oncology for the first pivotal trial of sac-TMT, which it licensed from Chengdu-based Sichuan-Kelun Pharmaceutical and whose revenue Merck hopes will offset expiring patents on the world's best-selling drug Keytruda. At the same Madrid meeting, Guangdong-based Akeso showed data on ivonescimab, which its licensee Summit Therapeutics hopes will supplant Keytruda.

At a Jefferies healthcare conference in June, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said: "The way I see it, by 2030 my competition will not be Merck and Lilly — it will be Chinese companies."

Almost 40% of drugs now in clinical trials — and about half of the cancer drugs — originated in China. American investors may be wondering how to catch a ride on China's wave of drug innovation.

Brokers can help you buy shares of Kelun, Akeso, and the other Chinese pharmas listed on Hong Kong's stock exchange. A few, like Zai Lab, have dual listings on Nasdaq.

For the foreseeable future, however, the answer will be right in front of you. America is where the world's drug companies make money. Regulatory and commercial savvy, not to mention geopolitics, will put much of the money from China's drug inventions in the pockets of the U.S.-listed companies that license and sell them.

That includes the big multinationals — Merck, GSK, Pfizer, Eli Lilly, AstraZeneca, Roche Holding, Bristol Myers Squibb — along with specialists like Summit. Many ventures made with Chinese ingredients will travel the world in a Western vehicle, like the Nasdaq-listed BeOne Medicines or Legend Biotech.

In September, China's government set a 2030 goal for a quarter of the world's breakthrough drugs to be Chinese, with at least five reaching blockbuster billion dollar annual sales.

Don't bet against them. In a decade, China's drug industry has gone from supplying chemicals and generic drugs to creating products that accounted for half of last year's global partnership or licensing deals — worth some $135 billion. It is easier to get a drug into human clinical trials in China than in the U.S., so China is one of the first places to learn if a new molecule works in people.

Hundreds of top-notch biotech firms cluster around cities like Shanghai, and they work hard. On a September tour of Chinese biotech centers, Goldman Sachs analyst Salveen Richter visited a company in the evening.

"It was like 10 o'clock at night and the people were all still working," Richter says. "I think they work six to seven days a week."

However swift their scientific ascent, Chinese companies don't yet feel ready to tackle regulation, sales and insurance in the country where global drug companies make their best profits. The U.S. accounted for half of last year's global prescription drug sales, according to the industry researchers IQVIA, while Europe contributed about 25% and China just 7%.

China's low drug prices, and its oversupply of competing companies and molecules, leaves much of its biotech industry gasping for profits. That may result in a shakeout, like the one expected for China's electric-vehicle industry Few drug discoverers have the wherewithal to take their products global. Well-capitalized U.S. and European firms have lots of licensing opportunities.

"We didn't yet see any company in China that was saying, 'Hey, I'm going to start to commercializing myself globally,'" says Richter's Goldman colleague Asad Haider. "They have chosen to partner."

The fast-growing, profitable Innovent Biologics is frequently mentioned as one of China's most likely to succeed on the world stage. Its recent license deals with the likes of Takeda Pharmaceutical, Lilly, and Pfizer could bring in as much as $34 billion, and represented about 30% of Chinese out-licensing.

Yet its CEO Michael Yu told journalists in September that his company still feels like a start-up when it comes to handling American reimbursement, insurance formularies, medical affairs, distribution, and marketing.

To gain experience, Innovent has demanded co-development and co-commercialization arrangements in five recent global license deals. Over the course of those drug approvals and launches, the Chinese company will gain know-how and a bigger share of U.S. profits than China-based innovators have previously enjoyed.

Another way for China's pharma firms to gain experience, and capture U.S. profits is with the so-called NewCo model in which they license proprietary drug candidates to a new, independent company, says H.C. Wainwright healthcare analyst Arthur He.

Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals has favored this strategy, in which it puts the foreign rights to a drug into an American business that is dormant but has a Nasdaq listing. Bolstered with fresh capital from venture backers like Bain Capital Life Sciences and Atlas Venture, the maneuver gives Hengrui a piece of what is essentially an American biotech start-up.

Earlier this year, Hengrui put its GLP-1 weight-loss assets into Kailera Therapeutics. An experimental drug for a genetic heart problem went into Braveheart Bio.

With this year's revival in biotech stocks, other Chinese firms are trying NewCos.

Hansoh Pharmaceutical Group is bringing a psoriasis drug to the Nasdaq-listed NextCure, which will become Avere Therapeutics. Qyuns Therapeutics put a Crohn's disease drug into Synlogic, soon to be renamed Caldera Therapeutics.

Wellington Management invested in private financing for Avere, Caldera and a few other firms. Such deals give Wellington access to Chinese innovation, says the money manager's head of private biotech investing, Nilesh Kumar.

These Nasdaq-listed plays will give public investors access, too.

The ventures aren't China-domiciled, so they may escape the geopolitical obstacles shadowing China-U. S. technology transfers. On Oct. 22, the U.S. Treasury proposed restrictions on American equity investment in Chinese biotech ventures — with an exemption that allows technology acquisition and licensing. But an analysis last week by the law firm Sidley suggests that some NewCos could be barred by the proposed rules.

These international complications may help explain why the first companies to turn Chinese innovations into global blockbusters took care to plant their roots abroad.

Legend Biotech is a New Jersey-based pure play on a cell therapy invented in China. Partnered with Johnson & Johnson, it will share over $2 billion in revenue this year from the Carvykti cancer treatment.

BeOne should see $5 billion in sales this year from Brukinsa, the cancer treatment invented 10 years ago in the company's Beijing lab. Last year, BeOne changed its name from Beigene and redomiciled to Switzerland.

Apart from these few pioneers, it will take some years before China-based drug developers challenge Pfizer and the other multinationals in global markets. Until then, Pfizer and its peers will continue licensing from prolific Chinese innovators like Suzhou-based CStone Pharmaceuticals, to fill the holes left by their own expiring patents.

Investors will have ample opportunity to pick their plays. Molecules licensed from China fuel some of the highest hopes in Big Pharma's pipelines, and their clinical-trial results will be widely reported.

At last month's ESMO conference, GSK, AstraZeneca, Bristol, and Takeda Pharaceutical presented new treatments for lung and stomach cancers. Those drugs were licensed from China.

Merck is betting big on sac-TMT, the guided chemo drug it licensed from Kelun. At ESMO it presented the first of 18 Phase 3 trials on the drug. In patients with endometrial cancer — an illness where available treatments do little good — there were one-third fewer deaths in those treated with sac-TMT.

Goldman's Haider estimates that Merck's peak annual sales of sac-TMT could approach $14 billion, in a decade.

That would be a nice reward for Merck investors, and for cancer patients.

By Steven M. Sears

We are the playthings of time and volatility.

Sometimes those inexorable forces coexist peacefully, and life — in and out of markets — is uneventful and even halcyon. Other times they furiously collide. When profound change is involved, as now, the collision can be so shocking that basic truths are easily forgotten.

Consider these observations not as philosophical meanderings but as a way to understand recent market activity, when lackluster earnings stripped hundreds of billions of dollars — and maybe more — from benchmark indexes and top stocks. Consider these observations as a way to understand recent market activity, when lackluster earnings stripped hundreds of billions of dollars — and maybe more — from benchmark indexes and top stocks. The Democratic electoral sweep of Congress has introduced even more uncertainty.

Intel sparked the powder keg last week when the chip maker issued weak fourth-quarter financial guidance after beating third-quarter earnings estimates. The stock fell 29% and sharply increased anxiety about when artificial intelligence would generate corporate profits and not just massive expenses. Google parent Alphabet worsened sentiment by reporting negative free cash flow (again), further panicking investors with news of AI spending and slower growth in its search-engine business. Apple's results this week have deepened concerns.

If bad news from AI leaders occurred a few months ago, investors might have dismissed it. But the year ends soon, and the investor class is heavily focused on annual bonuses, which form the bulk of their compensation. Rather than characterizing sour results as the cost of building AI — an innovation many investors, ironically, are using with great results — the selloff could be rooted in seasonal sentiment and positioning shifts. We don't think it means investors have profound doubts that AI is the technology of the future, and it's too early to make any snap decisions on what the election means for AI.

After all, the S&P 500 index remains about 3.1% away from its record high and is still up 10.6% this year. The historically high return supercharges the magic of compounding for long-term investors.

To our thinking, the declines are opportunities to buy blue-chip stocks and sell bearish cash-secured put options. If another paroxysm occurs — if the midterm election results weaponize Congress against Wall Street, say — the opportunity to buy more stocks and sell more puts will again be attractive.

Consider Alphabet. Shares recently fell from about $325 to $280. The stock is down 10.5% this year, though it has more than doubled over the past three.

For investors with long time horizons, episodic short-term volatility is an opportunity for time arbitrage. This strategy monetizes short-term stock weakness by selling options with an elevated fear premium, benefiting long-term investments. It expresses a belief that blue-chip stock weakness, over long periods, is usually a buying opportunity, provided the stock can be held for at least three to five years and ideally much longer.

With Alphabet at $280.03, sell the January $270 put for about $10.60.

If Alphabet is below the strike price at expiration, buy the stock. If the stock exceeds the strike at expiration, the put premium is kept. The risk is the stock falls far below the strike, which could happen if something else makes investors panic. To manage the risk of further declines, "leg into" the trade. If you want to buy 900 shares, for instance, sell three puts with different strike prices and similar or different expirations.

Because we think AI will profoundly change the world, and that anything that poses major changes to the status quo is definitionally volatile, a broader approach is also worthwhile. The State Street SPDR S&P 500 exchange-traded fund will almost certainly advance when AI fears lessen. To pre-position, buy bullish call options that expire in one to three months and are a bit higher than the ETF's price. If you also sell puts on the ETF, you should raise enough money to pay for some or all of the call.

Don't let volatility scare you. Over time, embracing it creates wealth.
